title: Rabies Data Raises New Questions About Vietnam’s Dog Meat Trade
excerpt: Vietnam’s rabies crisis, weak slaughter oversight, and public support point toward one locally backed health solution: ending the dog meat trade.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam recorded 164 animal rabies outbreaks and 51 human deaths by September 3, 2026, while dog-meat supply chains remain outside any registered slaughterhouse system. With 95% of Vietnamese supporting an end to the trade, stronger public-health action can follow local demand and protect people, families, and animals.

Key Findings

Rabies Spread Shows Cost of Weak Dog Control

Vietnam reported 164 rabies outbreaks across 129 communes and wards in 22 provinces and cities from the start of 2026 through September 3. Authorities destroyed 293 domestic animals, while 51 people died from rabies, according to reports citing national epidemiological data. Dong Thap reporting describes the scale of the outbreak and the need for vaccination and registration.

On September 7, a dog in Dak Lak tested positive after attacking four people. Local reporting shows why authorities need reliable records, vaccination coverage, and rapid response for every dog—not only animals linked to a bite.

Exposure Can Become Fatal Without Fast Treatment

Ho Chi Minh City recorded five rabies deaths during the first six months of 2026, with reports stating that all victims had not received post-exposure vaccine or serum after suspected dog or cat bites. A September health report links current dog attacks to continuing rabies risk.

Rabies prevention requires more than emergency treatment. It requires vaccination, traceability, humane handling, and safe slaughter standards. Hanoi CDC has warned residents not to slaughter, eat, or use meat or products from animals suspected of carrying rabies. The guidance places public safety before consumption.

Food Safety Rules Tighten, But Dog Meat Remains Unresolved

From September 1, 2026, Vietnam shifted state inspection of imported animal-origin foods toward provincial authorities. Ministry guidance reported in September shows government attention on inspection, quarantine, and accountability across food supply chains.

Yet the research found no confirmed national dog-meat ban and no dedicated September dog-meat safety incident. The gap matters: Vietnam has zero registered dog-meat slaughterhouses, leaving this supply chain completely unregulated. Rabies, E. coli, and Salmonella risks grow when authorities cannot verify origin, veterinary inspection, handling, or cold-chain controls.

Local Support Creates Public-Health Mandate

A 2021 survey found that 95% of Vietnamese support ending the dog meat trade. This is not an outside demand imposed on Vietnam. It is a locally supported change that aligns animal welfare with safer food systems, stronger disease control, and protection for families such as Lucky’s—beloved companions who deserve identification, vaccination, and care.

Ending the trade would also reduce incentives for dog theft and untraceable movement. A September 9 court report from Tay Ninh described convictions in a large dog-theft and resale case involving more than 1.6 tonnes of dogs. The court report records prison sentences for three defendants, including four years for the alleged ringleader.

Also Worth Noting

  • Da Nang improves control — An Khe Ward began inspections and directed captured stray dogs and cats to a municipal holding facility on September 10.
  • Cruelty enforcement advances — A Da Lat man received a VND2 million fine after a video showed him beating an Alaska Malamute.
  • Vaccination campaigns expand — Cu Lao Dung commune administered 550 emergency rabies vaccine doses in one campaign.
  • Slaughter oversight needs work — September reporting highlighted unresolved management issues involving veterinary medicines and slaughter inspection.
  • Food law remains in motion — Authorities continued preparing amendments to Vietnam’s Food Safety Law, without confirming a dog-meat ban.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030.
